prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and thereby transforming the analysis of the gains from trade

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed what trade economists treat as the unit of analysis. Gains from trade now operate through selection, reallocation across firms and the extensive margin, as well as through industry-level comparative advantage or scale. The framework is a theory that disciplines micro data. It explains exporter premia and the productivity effects of liberalisation, and it gave a shared language for a large empirical literature built on firm-level administrative and customs data. This combination of a clear conceptual advance with data-driven validation is what I value most. It matches my view that new data and an explanatory framework together make a prize-worthy contribution. The work is more than twenty years old and is standard in textbooks, empirical trade and policy evaluation, so maturity is not in doubt. Attribution is reasonably tractable: Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman's heterogeneous-firm work, including Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, supports a second laureate. A two-person prize keeps the credit concentrated on the core discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges. Empirical pioneers of firm-level trade facts and the parallel quantitative-trade line (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) are not credited on this ballot entry, and a prize to Melitz and Helpman could be read as under-crediting them. There is also a question of how distinct this advance is from the new trade theory already recognised in 2008. Finally, some welfare implications are sensitive to functional-form assumptions, so the gains-from-trade message is less robust than the qualitative selection result.

responses.point: Enflo ranks the political-economics trio (B009) first as a foundational, mature field that connects to historical and comparative work. She also ranks B026 second but worries that Krugman's 2008 prize may make firm heterogeneity look like an extension of recognised ground.
responses.response: I agree that B009 is mature and coherent. I ranked it second, and its three-name credit is cleaner than most. I still put B026 ahead of it for two reasons. First, the 2024 institutions prize is thematically adjacent, and the committee would need to argue distinctness. Second, the Persson-Tabellini constitutional results rest on weaker identification than the firm-level evidence in trade. On the Krugman point, I read the two advances as distinct. Krugman's work explained intra-industry trade and location with representative firms, whereas Melitz changed the unit of analysis to the heterogeneous firm and produced a new, empirically testable channel of reallocation. This is a later advance whose evidence base is micro data that did not exist for the earlier theory. I concede that the overlap question is real and that I cannot settle it from the written record alone.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the collateral-constraint and credit-cycle line (B007) first. He argues it is a core part of how macroeconomists understand cycles and crises, developed into a large quantitative literature on financial frictions, with Kiyotaki and Moore as clear originators.
responses.response: I accept that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is cleaner than almost any other on the list, and that the mechanism shaped post-2008 thinking. My hesitation is about evidence rather than importance. Several colleagues, including Strömberg and Teorell, note that identification of collateral channels is less clean than the theory. The 2022 prize partly covers the same ground. Credit between the Kiyotaki-Moore and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist lines is intertwined, which is why you consider adding Gertler. In trade, the mechanism was tested directly against firm-level data across many countries and has survived. That pushes me toward B026, but I would not call B007 an unreasonable choice, and I would keep it among serious alternatives if the committee wants a macro-finance award.

responses.point: Dreber ranks law and finance (B001) first for its large, durable empirical programme in finance, law and development. She also flags that causal interpretation, measurement choices and robustness of the cross-country regressions are concerns, and that Vishny's exclusion is a judgment call.
responses.response: I share your assessment of B001's breadth. It drew on newly assembled cross-country data and shaped policy debate, and I ranked it third. The concerns you list are, for me, the decisive difference. The causal reading of legal origins is contested, some indices have been revised, and the three-name cap forces the exclusion of a co-author of the foundational papers. Heavy citation does not settle whether the central claim has held up. B026's central claim, that selection and reallocation matter for aggregate productivity gains, has held up through replication across countries and datasets, even if the magnitudes are debated. I therefore treat the contested-identification problem you raise as a real cost for B001 relative to B026.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B026 second and treats Melitz (2003) as the clear originating model, with Helpman extending it and shaping the agenda. He regards Redding's extensions as important but more derivative, and notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this ballot entry.
responses.response: I agree with your attribution logic and it is the basis for my two-name proposal. I also share your concern about the uncredited empirical and quantitative contributors. The citation should therefore be written about the theoretical framework of heterogeneity and selection, rather than claiming to honour all firm-level trade research. Where we may differ is on Redding. I would hold him back under the cap because his quantitative and spatial work builds on the framework, but I recognise that this reads differently if the committee wants to credit the quantitative-trade extensions explicitly. I would want that argued on the merits and not just on the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would credit Bernard, Jensen, Eaton or Kortum, none of whom are on this ballot entry, for the empirical and quantitative parallels to the Melitz framework.
Whether Helpman or Redding is the better second or third laureate, and whether Helpman's broader trade record is better recognised under a different contribution.
How distinct the firm-heterogeneity advance is from the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
How sensitive the welfare and gains-from-trade implications are to the functional-form assumptions of the canonical models.
I have not independently verified citation or priority details; my assessments rest on the supplied evidence and my own reading of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in labour economics and the economics of crime, and my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) do not appear among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot entry.
